questions.q: Why does an ordinary Apex test, without System.runAs, typically fail to prove a sharing rule works correctly?
options: Apex tests cannot query Opportunity records at all
Apex normally runs in system mode, ignoring record-level sharing, so the test runs with elevated visibility regardless of sharing rules
Sharing rules only apply to Visualforce pages, never to Apex
Test methods are not allowed to insert User records
questions.explain: Outside of runAs (or classes using WITH USER_MODE / explicit sharing enforcement), Apex executes in system mode and ignores the running user's record sharing, so an ordinary test can't by itself prove sharing rules restrict visibility.

questions.q: What does System.runAs(user) { ... } actually enforce inside its block?
options: Both record sharing and object/field-level permissions
Record sharing (role hierarchy, sharing rules, manual sharing) — not object or field-level permissions by itself
Only field-level security, not sharing
Nothing — it is purely cosmetic and has no effect on query results
questions.explain: runAs switches the record-sharing context to the given user, so role hierarchy and sharing rules apply — but it does not by itself enforce object or field-level permissions.

questions.q: A test uses System.runAs to simulate a user with no field-level access to a particular field, then queries that field inside the runAs block without using WITH USER_MODE. What happens?
options: The query automatically throws a security exception
The field can still be returned, because runAs alone does not enforce field-level security
The entire test class fails to compile
The field is automatically masked with asterisks
questions.explain: Since runAs only switches sharing context and not permission enforcement, a field the user lacks access to can still come back from a plain query — proving field-level security requires an additional mechanism like WITH USER_MODE or Security.stripInaccessible.

options: Only inside test methods
Only inside triggers
Anywhere in Apex, including production business logic
Only inside Visualforce controllers
questions.explain: System.runAs has meaning and effect only inside test methods — it's a testing construct, not something used in regular business logic.

questions.q: Can multiple System.runAs blocks be used, and nested, within a single test method?
options: No, only one runAs call is allowed per test method
Yes, more than one runAs block can be used, including nesting, to switch between several simulated users
Only two runAs blocks are allowed per test class, not per method
runAs can only be called from a @TestSetup method
questions.explain: A test method can call runAs more than once, and runAs blocks can be nested, to simulate switching between multiple different users as the test progresses.
